summary: Defines the Multipart/Related MIME content type, a common way to represent objects made of related body parts, such as an HTML page with its images, and gives examples. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 2112.

eli5.summary: A single package for a main item and the extras that belong to it, such as a page and its pictures.

questions: how to embed images in html email
how to send compound objects in email
subtitle: A MIME content-type for sending related parts that make sense only together.

tldr.problem: Email systems need a way to send compound objects where multiple parts are interdependent: for example, an HTML page with embedded images, or data records with metadata. Individual MIME types handle single objects, but compound objects require a way to group and relate multiple parts.
tldr.mechanism: Multipart/Related wraps multiple MIME body parts and marks one (the root) as the primary object. The root is identified by a content-ID and the type parameter specifies what kind of object it is. Other parts are linked from within the root, making clear their relationship to the main object.
tldr.outcome: The specification provided a general-purpose mechanism for compound objects, reducing the need to define new multipart subtypes for each use case. It became widely used for HTML email with inline images and other related-content scenarios.

facts.label: Root identification
facts.value: By content-ID via start parameter, or first body part by default

today: RFC 1872 was replaced by RFC 2112 in 1997. Multipart/Related remains widely used for HTML email with inline images and other scenarios where a main object depends on related resources bundled in the same message.

sections.title: Introduction to Multipart/Related
sections.content:
Internet mail applications often need to send compound objects made up of multiple related components. MIME-PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail), MIME-Macintosh, and other applications require a way to group and send interdependent body parts.

Before this RFC, each new compound object type required defining a specific new multipart subtype. RFC 1872 proposes instead a single Multipart/Related content-type that can handle any compound object. The object is categorized by a type parameter specifying the root's MIME type. A start parameter identifies which body part is the root (by content-ID), and an optional start-info parameter can provide auxiliary information for processing.

With this approach, applications use one mechanism to handle the same goal across different purposes, following MIME's design philosophy.
sections.eli5: Different applications need to send objects made of multiple linked parts. Instead of creating a new type for each one, this document defines a single way to package any compound object and mark which part is the main one.

sections.title: Content-Type Parameters and Syntax
sections.content:
Multipart/Related messages have three parameters:

Type (required): Specifies the MIME media type of the root body part, such as text/html or application/x-fixedrecord. This parameter tells the application what it is dealing with before examining the root itself.

Start (optional): The content-ID of the root body part. If not present, the first body part in the message is the root. The content-ID uses the angle-bracket format from RFC 822, like <950118.AEBH@example.com>.

Start-Info (optional): Auxiliary information for processing, either as a text string or a reference to another part via content-ID. Applications define how they interpret this parameter.

The MIME syntax for these parameters is defined formally in the RFC, with the note that values often need quoting since they contain special characters like <, >, /, and @.
sections.eli5: The message tells the receiver: 'Type is the main type of object, Start points to which part is the main one, and Start-Info gives extra instructions for handling it.'

sections.title: Examples: HTML Pages and Custom Formats
sections.content:
The RFC gives two detailed examples. The first, Application/X-FixedRecord, sends a data stream along with a record-length list that describes how to parse it. The sender generates the length list on the fly and includes both parts in one message.

The second example shows Text/X-Okie, an imaginary markup language similar to HTML. An Okie document contains text with embedded images. The document is the root (type parameter is Text/X-Okie), and the images are separate body parts referenced by content-ID using the cid: URI scheme. When the receiver gets the message, the Okie application processes the main document and resolves the image references to the included image parts.

Both examples show how Multipart/Related lets a sending application package a compound object as a single message while keeping parts logically separate. The receiving application gets all the pieces and can process them as a unit.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending a web page and its pictures as one package. The page says 'image goes here' by referring to a picture by ID, and the pictures are sent along with the same IDs so the receiver knows which picture goes where.

sections.title: Processing and User Agent Requirements
sections.content:
User agents that receive Multipart/Related messages should recognize the content-type and pass all the message parts to an application that understands the type parameter. If a user agent does not recognize Multipart/Related, it falls back to treating it as Multipart/Mixed, sending each part separately to the user.

If a user agent recognizes Multipart/Related but cannot handle the specified type, it should either suppress the entire message or process just the root part, and inform the user of what happened.

Processing a Multipart/Related message differs from other media types because the parts cannot be handled independently. The application must process the compound object as a whole. A receiving agent (an intermediary between the MIME user agent and the final application) might parse the document and substitute local file names for the original sender's references to parts.

Since MIME is recursive, Multipart/Related messages can contain nested Multipart/Related structures. The outermost application is responsible for ensuring that any nested Multipart/Related entities are processed correctly.
sections.eli5: When the receiver gets the message, their email program should give all the parts to an application that knows how to handle that type of compound object. If the program doesn't know how to handle it, it just shows the main part or treats all parts as separate.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Multipart/Related messages require certain information to be available to the processing application:

  • The bodies of the MIME entities and all their headers
  • The parameters from the Multipart/Related header
  • The mapping between each part's local file name, its header data, and its content-ID

When Multipart/Related objects are stored (not just displayed), the internal linkages between parts may require processing. A receiving agent may need to update the root's internal references to point to local file names instead of the content-IDs used in transmission.

Email configuration systems may benefit from referring to Multipart/Related as Multipart/Related/<type>, where <type> is the value of the type parameter, making it clear what kind of compound object is being handled.
sections.eli5: The receiver needs to know the parts' contents, the headers, and which part is which. If storing the object, it might need to fix up the references inside the root to point to where the parts are saved locally.
